questions.q: The page opens on Proxima Cen b. How far away is it, and how was it found?
questions.do: Read the planet panel on the right (the big name shows Proxima Cen b). Look at Distance and Found by.
questions.a: About 4.2 light-years. It was found by Radial Velocity in 2016, so the note warns that its radius is an estimate from its mass.

questions.q: Kepler-22 b gets almost the same starlight as Earth. Why is it not in the "Rocky size, Earth-like starlight" table?
questions.do: Type Kepler-22 in the search box and click Kepler-22 b. Read Radius and Starlight received. Then read the rule above the table.
questions.a: Its starlight is about 1.01 × Earth, which fits. But its radius is about 2.10 × Earth. The table only takes planets between 0.5 and 1.6 Earth radii, so it is too big to count as rocky size.

questions.q: Compare the trip to Proxima Cen b with the trip to TRAPPIST-1 e on a 1 g ship.
questions.do: Read 1 g ship, crew time for Proxima Cen b. Then search TRAPPIST-1, click TRAPPIST-1 e and read the same row and its Distance.
questions.a: Proxima Cen b: about 3.5 years for the crew (4.2 light-years). TRAPPIST-1 e: about 7.3 years (about 40.5 light-years). The distance is nearly 10 times bigger, but the crew time only doubles, because the ship keeps speeding up for half the trip, and relativity makes the crew age far less than people at home.

questions.q: TRAPPIST-1 e is smaller than Earth. Why does it dim its star far more than Earth dims the Sun?
questions.do: Select TRAPPIST-1 e and read the note under Watch it transit. Compare its dip with the sentence about Earth crossing the Sun.
questions.a: It blocks about 0.50% of the light. Earth blocks the Sun by only 84 ppm (0.0084%). The dip is (planet radius ÷ star radius)², and TRAPPIST-1 is a tiny star, only about 0.12 solar radii. So a small planet covers a big part of it.

questions.q: Look up 51 Peg b. How and when was it found, and how does the discoveries chart show that history?
questions.do: Search 51 Peg and click 51 Peg b. Read Found by. Then look at the Discoveries by year chart and its label.
questions.a: 51 Peg b was found by Radial Velocity in 1995. The discoveries chart starts in 1992 with only a few planets a year. Its label reads PEAK: 2016, credited to Kepler: the peak year, credited to the Kepler telescope.
